transcript.text: Mr. Lincoln. The ethics of this chamber require that no member profit from legislation he has a hand in passing. You are well-regarded here, sir, but I must hear your account. Explain yourself.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
Mr. Lincoln, your account of the bill's legislative journey is noted. However, the charges brought by Representative Douglas do not concern the political affiliations of those who introduced or passed the bill, nor the Governor who signed it. The *charge* is that *you*, a member of this body, cast a vote in favor of a land grant while simultaneously representing the principal beneficiary of that very grant in your legal practice.

The ethics of this chamber are clear: a member must not profit, directly or indirectly, from legislation they have a hand in passing. I must ask you again, sir, how do you reconcile your vote for the Sangamon County land grant with your representation of its primary recipient? Did you or your practice receive remuneration for this representation?

transcript.text: I can answer that question by stating that I have received no pecuniary compensation for my legal services to Mr. Bell on any matter whatever. That answer will doubtless satisfy the demands of honorable gentlemen, but there is another point upon which I think it fair to inquire. The lands to which the grant is made are not located in Illinois. They lie beyond the Mississippi River, within the borders of Missouri. To the best of my knowledge, the grant has never been received there. Inasmuch as it cannot be placed of use within the State, it might possibly be supposed that it amounts to nothing more than a mere gift, or perhaps to a loan, to Mr. Bell. Now, I know that there have been many attempts, both before and since this grant was made, to secure a position for a Western military post within easy distance of those lands. That such attempts have been made I know from the fact that my partner, Mr. Dyer, was authorized by the War Department to go West and look out for a site for such a post. I know also that the General Government have granted those lands to Mr. Bell under a condition that they shall be used as a military post. All these facts seem to me to go together, and make it appear that what we have really done is to give the Government of the United States title to a tract of land, which is to be used as a military post, and which may possibly be given to Mr. Bell to farm. Now, I think it can be fairly said that if any man has an interest in that军事要地, it is Mr. Bell. And that interest is not merely personal. If those lands are ever needed for a military purpose, the honor and glory of their acquisition will be his. Whether that will be in the near or the distant future, I cannot say, but it is quite certain that it will be. And now, gentlemen, I am willing to leave this question with you.
